Workspace

SVGCraft is laid out like Photoshop: menus along the top, the tool's options under them, tools down the left, panels down the right, and your drawings in tabs in the middle. It edits on tablets and larger screens; a phone gets a preview to look at drawings.

On a phone

Look at, check and share SVGs on your phone. A phone gets a preview, not the editor, so nothing you do there changes a drawing.

  • Tap Open (the folder) to open an SVG. Each opens in a tab of its own; tap a tab to switch, or swipe along the tab bar for the next or previous drawing (while all the tabs fit).
  • Drag to pan and pinch to zoom. Tap Fit (the four corners) to fit the drawing to the screen.
  • Double-tap the canvas to zoom in on that spot (to 100%, or twice the fit for small drawings), and double-tap again to fit.

The phone toolbar

  • Play (▶): plays the drawing's animations. ■, or a tap on the button, stops them. It's greyed out when nothing is animated.
  • Layers: the layer list, to show and hide layers while you look (see below).
  • Text view (</>): the SVG source full-screen, syntax-coloured, to read (long lines wrapped), search and Copy (or download). The same button, now a picture, goes back to the drawing.
  • Background: the artwork on the checkerboard, white or black. Each tap moves to the next, and the button shows which it's on: a checkered circle, white ringed in black, or black ringed in white. It's remembered.
  • Share: the phone's share sheet, with the SVG and a PNG of it. Where the browser can't share files, the SVG is downloaded instead.
  • Info (ⓘ): the drawing's details (file, size, dimensions, layers, animations, fonts) and its metadata from File Info (title, author, description, keywords, date, copyright, licence and source, linked), read-only. Help opens this guide, and About SVGCraft is at the bottom.

Showing and hiding layers

  • Tap Layers, then a layer's eye to hide or show it. Each layer has a preview, always on the checkerboard as in the Layers panel.
  • Hide all and Show all do every layer. Show all includes layers the file itself hides.
  • Layers inside a hidden group are dimmed: they can't show until the group does.
  • Only the preview changes. Nothing is saved, and switching tab or moving to a bigger screen shows the drawing as it is again.

Good to know

  • A phone is a screen narrower than 768 px, or a phone held sideways.
  • The editing tools, menus and panels are hidden there, and so is Undo.

On a tablet

Edit on a tablet as on a computer. In landscape the layout is the same as on a computer; in portrait it makes room for the canvas.

  • The toolbar moves to the bottom of the screen.
  • Tap the sliders button (top right) to slide the panels in from the right, and again to put them away.

Good to know

  • This layout is for any window narrower than 1024 px, such as a tablet in portrait. The theme button and the Export label are hidden there to save room.

Offline and as an app

Use SVGCraft without a connection, or in a window of its own like any other app.

  1. Open SVGCraft from the web once. From then on it works offline too.
  2. To install it: in Chrome and Edge, click the install icon in the address bar, or choose File → Install SVGCraft…. On an iPhone or iPad, tap Share → Add to Home Screen.
  3. Open it from your apps. It opens in a window of its own.

Updates

SVGCraft looks for a newer version by itself whenever the internet is there: when it starts, when it comes back online, when you come back to its window, and every hour while it's open.

  1. When there's a newer version, a bar at the bottom of the window says so.
  2. Click Update to reload SVGCraft with the new version. Your open drawings, their tabs and their * marks are kept.
  3. Or click Later to carry on. It isn't offered again by itself until there's a newer version still; Help → Check for Updates… shows it again.

Help → Check for Updates… looks at once and says what it found: up to date (with the version), a new version (the bar), or no connection.

Good to know

  • On desktop Chrome and Edge, the installed app can be chosen to open .svg files.
  • Install SVGCraft… only shows in the File menu when the browser offers to install it.
  • Offline use works through a service worker, which keeps SVGCraft's files. Opened straight from disk (file://), none of this applies, and there are no updates.
  • The version is a short code made from SVGCraft's files (src/version.js): any change to the app gives a new one. Online, a page you open always loads the newest files, so the bar matters for a window left open, or one started while offline.

The editor window

Find your way round the editor. From top to bottom:

  • Menu bar: File, Edit, Image, Layer, Object, Type, Select, View, Window and Help (see The menu bar).
  • Options bar: the settings for the current tool (see The options bar).
  • Toolbar, down the left (see The toolbar).
  • Document tabs above the canvas, one per open drawing, showing the file name and zoom (see Documents).
  • Panels, down the right (see Docked panels).
  • Status bar, along the bottom: an editable zoom field, the document size, and hints for the current tool.

The menu bar

Find every command, in Photoshop's order.

  • Click a menu to open it, then hover to switch between menus. The arrow keys move around too.
  • An item that can't run on the current selection is greyed out. Its tooltip still shows, and its shortcut does nothing until it can run.

What needs what

  • Crop to Selection needs a selection.
  • A Clipping Mask, Combine Shapes or Text on Path needs two layers.
  • Distribute needs three.

Good to know

  • Layer holds what works on whole layers: New, Duplicate, Layer Style, Clipping Mask, Group, Arrange, Align, Lock and Merge.
  • Object holds symbols and what works on shapes: Path, Combine Shapes and Flip.

Right-click menus

Reach what the selection can do without going to the menu bar, as in Photoshop.

  • Right-click a layer on the canvas: it's selected (unless it's already in the selection) and the menu lists what the selection can do: Cut, Copy, Duplicate, Free Transform, Transform, Arrange, Align, Group, Clipping Mask, Combine Shapes, symbols, Layer Style and Lock, then Play Animations, Deselect, Select Inverse and Crop to Selection.
  • Layers Here (at the top, when more than one layer is under the pointer) lists them, top first, so you can pick one that's covered by others. The ticked one is selected.
  • Right-click empty canvas with nothing selected: Paste, Select All, Crop to Drawing, Play Animations and the zoom commands.
  • Play Animations (when the drawing has any) plays them on the canvas, as ▶ Play does; while they play, right-click → Stop Animations. A right-click doesn't stop them, as a click does.
  • During Free Transform: Scale, Rotate, Skew, the turns and flips, and Commit or Cancel Transform.
  • While editing text: the browser's own menu, for cutting, copying and pasting the text.
  • In the Layers panel: see Right-click a layer.

Good to know

  • The menu only lists what would do something now, rather than greying out the rest, to keep it short: Ungroup appears for a group, Create Outlines for text, Image Trace for an image, Distribute for three layers or more; Arrange offers only the ways the layer can move (no Bring Forward on the top layer); Copy Layer Style needs a style; Select Inverse needs layers left unselected; 100% shows when you're not at 100%.
  • Paste is always there: what's on the clipboard can't be known until the browser is asked to read it.
  • Each item is the menu bar's own, with its shortcut, so the menu teaches the keys.
  • Arrow keys move through it, → opens a submenu, Enter runs, Esc closes.

The options bar

Change how the current tool works. The bar shows the settings for the tool you have: stroke width and smoothing for the pencil, mode and size for the eraser, or the point commands for Edit Points.

  • Type a value, or drag a field's label sideways to scrub it. Shift scrubs 10× faster.
  • When the window is too narrow for all of a tool's settings, a › at the bar's end (and ‹ once you've scrolled) shows there's more: click it, or scroll the bar with the mouse wheel.

Auto-Select (Move tool)

  • Group: a click on the canvas picks the whole top-level item.
  • Layer: a click picks the exact shape under the cursor, even deep inside groups.

The toolbar

Pick a tool, and the colours it paints with.

  • Click a tool to use it.
  • A small corner mark means more tools share its button. Hold the button down, right-click it, Alt-click it or click the mark to pick another from its flyout.
  • Click the fill or stroke chip (at the bottom) to make it the active paint. Click it again to pick a colour.
  • Above the chips, as in Photoshop: the little black-and-white squares set the default colours (D: black fill, white stroke), and the curved arrow swaps fill and stroke (X).

Pointers

The pointer shows what a click will do, as in Photoshop:

  • the Move tool's arrow and cross;
  • Edit Points' white arrow;
  • a cross or lasso for picking points, with + while Shift adds and − while Alt takes away;
  • the pen's nib, with * to start a path and o over its first point to close it;
  • the pencil, the eyedropper and the type I-beam;
  • the curved arrow on the rotate handle.

Docked panels

Keep the panels you use open beside the canvas, sized and folded the way you like.

  • Click a tab's icon to open it. The open tab also shows its name, and hovering any tab names it.
  • Drag the divider under a group to resize it. Double-click the divider for the group's natural height, or focus it and use the arrow keys.
  • Double-click a group's tab bar, or click the chevron at its end, to fold it to just its tabs. Layers then gets the room. Click a tab to open it again.
  • Click » above the panels to shrink the column to a strip of icons, leaving more room for the canvas. Click « to bring the panels back.
  • With the panels as icons, click an icon to pop its panel out beside the strip. A click elsewhere, or Esc, puts it away.

The panels

  • Color: the fill and stroke, with the stroke's width, alignment, caps, joins and dashes.
  • Properties, Character, Paragraph, Animation and History. Properties has the selection's Transform (X, Y, W and H, typed in the document's units, with a link to keep the proportions), the shape's settings, the document size, and the grid and snap.
  • Selecting text shows the Character tab; selecting something else afterwards goes back to the tab you had.
  • Layers: see Layers.
  • Swatches, gradients, patterns and symbols are made and managed in the Libraries window (Window → Libraries).

Good to know

  • Each group keeps its height whatever its tab shows, as in Photoshop. Longer content scrolls inside it, so selecting something never shuffles the panels below.
  • Layers takes the rest of the height and always keeps room.
  • Heights and folded groups are remembered for your next visit. Window → Reset Workspace puts them back.

Window menu

Open any panel by name, or put the workspace back as it was.

  • Choose a panel to open it on its tab. This brings the panels back if Tab hid them, or pops it out of the icon strip.
  • Choose a ticked panel to fold it away. A tick means it's showing.

Options

  • Libraries: opens or closes the Libraries window.
  • SVG Source (Ctrl+U) and Icon Preview (Ctrl+Alt+P): open or close them (see Split view).
  • Collapse Panels to Icons: the icon strip.
  • Hide Panels (Tab): hides the panels, and Tab brings them back.
  • Reset Workspace: every panel open on its first tab, the icon strip and hiding undone, SVG Source, Icon Preview and Libraries docked at the standard widths, and dialogs back where they first open.

Split view

Watch the SVG source or the Icon Preview beside your drawing as you work.

  1. Choose Window → SVG Source or Window → Icon Preview. It docks in a column beside the canvas.
  2. Drag the divider at the column's left to resize it, or focus the divider and use the arrow keys.
  3. With both open they stack, Icon Preview above SVG Source. Drag the divider between them to share the height.

Libraries docks in a column of its own, between this column and the panels.

Good to know

  • The button in each one's title bar floats it as a window of its own, and docks it back.
  • Whether each is docked, the column's width and the split are remembered.
  • In windows narrower than 1024 px they float.

Rulers, guides and smart guides

Line things up exactly: drag guides out of the rulers, and let shapes snap to them and to each other.

  1. Drag from the top or left ruler onto the canvas to make a guide.
  2. Drag a guide with the Move tool to reposition it (Shift rounds to 10 px), or drag it back onto a ruler to delete it.
  3. Move or draw near a guide, and it snaps there. With Smart Guides on, it also snaps to the edges and centres of other objects and of the artboard, and magenta lines show what lined up.

Rulers

  • Rulers run along the top and left, in document pixels. Their ticks re-scale with zoom, and a marker follows the cursor.
  • View → Rulers (Ctrl+R) turns them off.

Guides

  • View → New Guide… places a guide at an exact position.
  • Show Guides (Ctrl+;), Lock Guides (Ctrl+Alt+;), Snap to Guides and Clear Guides are in the View menu too.
  • Guides are part of undo.

Snapping

  • A moved selection snaps by its left, centre or right edge, and by its top, middle or bottom.
  • A guide or smart match within 6 screen pixels takes priority over the grid.
  • Hold Ctrl/⌘ while dragging to skip snapping.

In the file

  • Guides are saved in the file as invisible metadata (data-sc-guides on the root <svg>), which renders nothing.

SVGCraft Help

Look up how to do something, from anywhere in SVGCraft.

  • Choose Help → SVGCraft Help (F1) to open this guide in its own tab, with every feature listed down the side and a search box.
  • Click the ? in a dialog's title bar, or a panel's tab bar, to open the topic for it.
  • Press F1 with a dialog open to go to that dialog's topic.
  • On a phone, Info has a Help button.

Theme

Choose a dark or light editor.

  • Click the sun / moon button at the top right to switch between dark and light. (It's hidden in windows narrower than 1024 px.)
  • Or choose View → Match System, Dark or Light.
  • SVGCraft follows your system's setting until you choose, and remembers your choice.

Features

Import

Bring artwork into SVGCraft: a whole drawing to edit, or an SVG or bitmap to add to the one you're working on.

  • File → Open… (Ctrl+O) → opens an SVG as a drawing of its own, in a new tab.
  • File → Import… → places an SVG (as a group, scaled to fit) or a PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF into the current drawing.
  • Drag and drop files onto the window → the same, without the menu.
  • Edit → Paste (Ctrl+V) → pastes SVG markup or an image from the clipboard. Edit → Cut and Copy put the selection on the clipboard as SVG.

Good to know

Every SVG that comes in (opened, imported, pasted, restored from this browser, or in a library file) is sanitised with an allowlist, because it goes into the editor's own page:

  • Only SVG drawing elements are kept: no script, foreignObject, or elements from other namespaces (such as HTML <base>, <form> or <meta>).
  • The file's own animation elements never enter the page either. Those that do what an animation preset does become that preset (see Animate); the others are left out, and a message says how many.
  • Event handlers (on*) are removed.
  • Links may only point inside the file, except image data: URLs and http(s) / mailto on <a>. They're checked as the browser reads them, so a hidden tab can't disguise javascript:.
  • url(…) that would fetch from another server is dropped from styles and paint attributes, so opening a file never contacts anyone.
  • <style> rules are baked into style attributes, so they can't restyle the editor. <title> and <desc> keep their text only.
  • Root-level paint like fill="none" stroke="currentColor" (common in icon sets) is pushed down to the shapes, so it survives.

Units and page size

Work in millimetres, inches or points, or set the drawing to a standard paper or screen size.

  1. Open the Properties panel. The Document settings are at the bottom.
  2. Pick the Units you want to see and type lengths in.
  3. Pick a Page size from the menu beside Units to resize the artboard to it, or type a W and H of your own.
  4. Click ↻ beside the page size to turn the page between portrait and landscape.

Settings

  • Units: pixels, millimetres, centimetres, inches or points. They're used by the rulers, W and H, guide positions, the X/Y/W/H transform fields, Image and Canvas Size, the grid and the status bar. The grid takes a round size in the new units (5 mm, ¼ in…).
  • Page size: A5, A4, A3, US Letter, Legal, Tabloid, business card, Full HD or square post. It also sets its units, and keeps the artboard's orientation.
  • W and H: the artboard's size, anchored top-left.

Good to know

  • Strokes, type and effects stay in pixels, as in Photoshop.
  • Inside, the drawing is always in pixels (96 per inch), so changing units changes nothing but the numbers.
  • A drawing in mm, cm, in or pt is saved with its real-world width and height (width="210mm"), so print, laser-cutter and plotter software know its size. The viewBox stays in pixels.
  • Opening a file sized in real units shows it in those units. One drawn in other units (a viewBox in mm, say) is scaled to pixels, keeping its real size. Plain pixel sizes are left as they were.

Image Trace…

Turn a bitmap (a logo, icon, scan or line drawing) into vector shapes you can edit.

  1. Place the image (File → Import…, or drop it on the canvas) and select it.
  2. Choose Image → Image Trace…. It's greyed out until an image is selected (see "What counts as an image", below).
  3. Pick the Preset closest to your image, then adjust the settings while you watch the preview. The line under the preview gives the result's colours, shapes and size.
  4. Click Trace. Each colour becomes its own layer in an "Image Trace" group, named like "Colour #2563eb · 34%".

Settings

  • Preset: Logo (up to 12 colours, background left out), Illustration (16), Photo (24, posterised) or Sketch (black and white). Changing a setting below switches it to Custom.
  • Colour / Greyscale / B&W: trace in colour, in greys, or in pure black and white at a Threshold you set.
  • Colours, up to: a maximum. Colours that look the same merge, so a flat logo keeps exactly the colours it has.
  • Ignore specks under: drops shapes smaller than this (noise, JPEG artefacts).
  • Smoothness: how much outlines are smoothed into curves. 0 gives pixel-exact polygons; real corners stay sharp at any setting.
  • Stacked (on by default): the largest colour goes at the bottom and each layer also covers every colour above it, so the layers overlap and no hairline gaps show. Turn it off for shapes that just touch, each only its own colour.
  • Recognise circles, ellipses and rectangles (on by default): an outline within about a pixel of one becomes a true ellipse or a rectangle (with rounded corners when they fit better). Blobs under 12 px aren't taken for boxes.
  • Ignore background: leaves out the colour round the edge of the image, where it touches the edge.
  • Keep the image (hidden): keeps the original under the trace, hidden, instead of replacing it.

What counts as an image

Select one layer that draws exactly one picture:

  • An image layer, or a group holding one (the trace goes into the group, beside the image).
  • A <use> of an image or a symbol: an image kept in <defs> and drawn by reference, as other apps export it, or a symbol instance whose symbol holds one image. The trace replaces the instance, where it's drawn; the symbol itself is left alone.
  • A shape filled with an image pattern, such as Figma's image fills. The pattern's first tile is traced where it's drawn, whole: it isn't cut to the shape's outline, and repeats of the tile aren't traced.

A symbol or group drawing several images asks you to pick one in the Layers panel.

When it won't trace

When Image Trace can't read the picture, it says why above the status bar (and in the browser's console):

  • "linked from elsewhere": the picture isn't embedded in the drawing. Import the image file itself (File → Import…).
  • "damaged, or in a format this browser can't read": the picture data doesn't decode. Re-export it as PNG or JPEG and import that.
  • "completely transparent": there are no visible pixels to trace.
  • Locked: an image locked with Lock all is refused; unlock it first.
  • "Nothing left to trace with these settings" in the dialog: lower Ignore specks under, or turn off Ignore background (on a picture that's mostly one colour, that colour is the background).
  • If the background thread fails, tracing carries on in the page (a note goes to the console), just a little slower.

Good to know

  • Best for logos, icons, illustrations, scans and line art. Photos come out posterised.
  • Each colour is taken from the solid inside of its areas, not their blended edges, so flat colours come out exact, and thin slivers of in-between colour along anti-aliased edges fold into their neighbours.
  • It reduces the image to a few colours (k-means in Lab, so similar-looking colours group together), traces each colour's outline and fits curves to it. Images are traced at 400–1000 px on the long side, in a background thread, so the page doesn't stall.

Image Size…

Make the whole drawing bigger or smaller: the artboard and everything on it.

  1. Choose Image → Image Size… (Ctrl+Alt+I).
  2. Type a new Width or Height, in the document's units or in percent.
  3. Click OK. It's one undo step.

Settings

  • Constrain proportions: change the width and the height follows, and the other way round.
  • Scale effects (on by default, Photoshop's Scale Styles): scales layer-effect distances and sizes too (shadow, glow, blur).

Good to know

  • It's SVG, so nothing is resampled or blurred.
  • Each top-level layer gets the scale on top of its transform, so strokes, text, patterns and gradients scale with the shapes. Guides scale too.
  • Animation distances always follow the art.

Canvas Size…

Add room round the drawing, or trim it, without scaling anything.

  1. Choose Image → Canvas Size… (Ctrl+Alt+C).
  2. Type a new Width and Height.
  3. Click an Anchor square for the part that stays put.
  4. Click OK.

Settings

  • Relative: the numbers are added to the current size (or trimmed with a minus) instead of replacing it.
  • Anchor: the centre grows or trims every side equally. A corner or an edge keeps that side fixed.

Good to know

  • Content and guides shift by whole pixels and the view follows, so nothing jumps on screen.
  • Whatever ends up outside the artboard is kept, just not exported.
  • The W and H in Properties → Document also resize the artboard, anchored top-left.

Grayscale and black & white

Turn a drawing, or just some layers, grey or pure black and white, as in Photoshop. The colours themselves change, so the saved SVG really is grey.

  1. Select the layers to change, or select nothing to change the whole drawing.
  2. Choose one from the Image menu (below).
  3. In a dialog, adjust it while the drawing previews, then click OK.

Options

  • Image → Adjustments → Desaturate (Shift+Ctrl+U): every colour to the grey of the same lightness. No dialog.
  • Image → Adjustments → Black & White… (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+B): Photoshop's six hue sliders (Reds, Yellows, Greens, Cyans, Blues, Magentas) and its defaults, previewed live. Default puts the sliders back.
  • Image → Adjustments → Threshold…: pure black and white, split at a Level you set, previewed live.
  • Image → Mode → Grayscale: the brightness the eye sees. No dialog.

Good to know

  • They change fills, strokes, gradient stops, patterns, symbols and markers in use, Layer Style colours and embedded images, pixel by pixel.
  • A gradient, pattern or symbol shared with layers outside the selection gets a copy of its own first, so only the selection changes.
  • Each is one undo step.
  • Layers locked against all edits, and linked (not embedded) images, are left as they are.

Crop

Fit the artboard tightly round your artwork, with no empty margin.

  • Image → Crop to Selection → the artboard fits round the selected layers.
  • Image → Crop to Drawing → the artboard fits round everything visible.

Good to know

  • The box is rounded out to whole pixels, and it's what's actually painted, so nothing is shaved off. Stroke width and position (Center, Inside, Outside), mitre tips at sharp corners (up to the mitre limit), square and round caps, round joins and effects (drop shadow, outer glow, blur) all count, including on rotated and scaled layers.
  • Hidden layers don't count.
  • The drawing and the guides shift so the artboard still starts at 0, 0, and nothing moves on screen.
  • Anything left outside the artboard is kept, but it isn't exported.
  • Define Pattern and Copy as SVG frame the selection the same way.

Select menu

Select everything, nothing, or everything you haven't selected.

  • Select → All (Ctrl+A) → selects every layer.
  • Select → Deselect (Ctrl+D, or Esc) → selects nothing.
  • Select → Inverse (Shift+F7, or Ctrl+Shift+I where the browser allows it) → selects every visible layer that wasn't selected.

Good to know

  • If the selection includes a shape inside a group, Inverse works with individual shapes. Otherwise it works with top-level layers.

History panel

Go back to any earlier point in your work, as in Photoshop.

  1. Open the panel with Window → History.
  2. Click a step to go back to it. The steps after it dim.
  3. Redo brings dimmed steps back, until a new change replaces them.

Good to know

  • It lists every step since the drawing was opened.
  • Each step is named by what made it: the menu command or shortcut, the tool you dragged with, or the panel control you changed.

Documents

Start a new drawing at the size you need: a screen, a social post, a phone or a sheet of paper.

  1. Choose File → New…, or click + in the tab bar.
  2. Pick a category and a preset, or type a Width and Height in any Units.
  3. Set the Name, the orientation (Portrait or Landscape) and the Background.
  4. Click Create (or press Enter, or double-click a preset). The drawing opens in a new tab.

Every open drawing gets a tab, as in Photoshop: see Open, close and switch tabs, Save and Save As and Export.

Presets

  • Recent: the last five sizes you made.
  • Web: common screen and ad sizes.
  • Social: Instagram, stories, X, link previews, YouTube and LinkedIn.
  • Mobile: iPhone, Android, iPad and Apple Watch.
  • Print: A5–A2, US Letter, Legal, Tabloid, business card, postcard and poster.

Settings

  • Background: Transparent, or a White, Black or custom colour. A colour becomes a "Background" layer at the bottom, locked in place as in Photoshop. Recolour it, or unlock and delete it.
  • Icon templates…: switches to New Icon, for app and toolbar icons.

Good to know

  • The dialog remembers your last settings.

Open, close and switch tabs

Work on several drawings at once, each in its own tab.

  • File → Open… (Ctrl+O) → the file opens in a tab of its own. An untouched Untitled tab is reused. File → Open Recent lists the files you've had open lately (see Open Recent).
  • File → New from Text… → a tab made from SVG code you paste (see Edit the source and New from Text).
  • Click a tab → switch to that drawing. Each tab keeps its own drawing, undo history and zoom.
  • Click a tab's ✕, middle-click it, or choose File → Close → closes the drawing. If it has unsaved changes, you're asked first: Save (the default) saves it, then closes it; Don't Save closes it without its changes; Cancel keeps it open.
  • A * after the name → the drawing differs from the version last opened or saved.

Good to know

  • Save (Ctrl+S) clears the *, as does the Export download. Undoing back to the saved version clears it too. PNG export doesn't count as saving.
  • A drawing opens fitted to the window. It stays fitted while the canvas changes size (a pane docking, panels folding, the window resized, a phone turned) until you zoom or pan it yourself. A fitted drawing comes back fitted, whatever size the window is then.
  • Closing the last tab leaves a blank workspace, as in Photoshop. Only New, Open (or dropping a file on it) and the view settings work until a drawing is open, and it stays blank after a reload.

Open Recent

Get back to a file you've worked on lately without hunting for it.

  1. Choose File → Open Recent.
  2. Click a file's name → it opens in a tab of its own. If it's already open, its tab comes forward instead.

Settings

  • Clear Recent File List → empties the list.

Good to know

  • The list holds the last 10 files you opened (File → Open…, dropped on the window, or opened with the installed app) or saved with Save As…, newest first. It's kept in this browser, so it's still there after a reload.
  • In Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers the list points at the files themselves: a file opens as it is now, and Save goes back to it. The browser may ask once a session before letting the page read it again. A file that's been moved or deleted since is taken off the list.
  • Browsers that can't reach files later (Firefox, Safari, phones) keep a copy of each file as it was opened instead (up to 5 MB each).

Save and Save As

Keep your drawing as an SVG file that reopens with everything editable.

  • File → Save (Ctrl+S) → saves the drawing. A new drawing asks where to save it the first time.
  • File → Save As… (Ctrl+Shift+S) → saves to a new file, and carries on there.

Good to know

  • In Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers, a drawing opened from a file (File → Open, dropped on the window, or opened with the installed app) saves straight back to that file. The browser asks once a session before letting the page change it.
  • The link to the file is kept with the drawing in this browser, so Save still goes back to it after a reload.
  • Browsers that can't write to files (Firefox, Safari, phones) download the SVG instead. There the menu says Download SVG, and Save As… isn't shown.

Kept in this browser

  • All open drawings are kept in this browser (IndexedDB) as they change. A reload or a later visit brings back the same tabs, the same * marks and the same view.
  • Keeping waits for a pause in your changes, but closing or reloading the page keeps them at once, so even the last change survives.
  • The browser's copy is per browser and per machine: Save to keep a file.
  • A drawing autosaved by an older version of SVGCraft is brought over as a tab.

Export

Get your drawing out as a file or onto the clipboard, for use elsewhere.

  • The Export button (top right) → downloads the drawing as SVG.
  • File → Export PNG @1×, @2× or @4× → downloads a PNG with a transparent background.
  • File → Copy as SVG markup → puts the drawing (or the selection) on the clipboard as SVG markup.
  • File → Export Clean SVG… → plain SVG for the web: see Export Clean SVG….

Export Clean SVG…

Save plain SVG for the web or another app, without SVGCraft's editing data.

  1. Choose File → Export Clean SVG….
  2. Set the options (they're remembered).
  3. Click Export. It saves <name>.min.svg.

Keep Save for your working copy: a clean SVG reopens as plain shapes.

Options

  • Decimal places for coordinates (2 by default). Path data is compacted too.
  • Minify (on by default): one line, with short ids.
  • Scale to fit (on by default): only a viewBox, no width and height.
  • Leave out hidden layers (on by default).
  • Keep File Info (on by default): the title, description and licence.
  • Solid colours as currentColor: for one-colour icons a page can recolour with CSS.

Good to know

  • It draws exactly the same: effects, clips, masks, gradients and patterns stay as the real SVG that draws them.
  • It leaves out what SVGCraft keeps to reopen the file editable: every data-* attribute (layer names, locks, effect settings, guides…), unreferenced ids, unused defs, comments, empty and attribute-free groups, and attributes set to their defaults.

Shape tools

Draw rectangles, ellipses, triangles, polygons, stars, lines and arrows, or any shape from the Symbols library.

  1. Pick a Shape tool (U). The toolbar shows one Shape button, the last tool used: hold it, right-click it or Alt-click it for the flyout.
  2. Set its options in the options bar: Radius for a rectangle, Sides and Star ratio for a polygon, Arrowheads for a line, Shape for a custom shape.
  3. Drag a box on the canvas. Shift makes the sides equal (a line snaps to 45°), and Alt draws from the centre.

The tools

  • Rectangle (R): see Rounded rectangles for its corners.
  • Ellipse (O).
  • Triangle.
  • Polygon: Sides, and a Star ratio below 100% pulls every other point in to make a star.
  • Line (L): Arrowheads at the Start, the End or both.
  • Custom Shape: any shape from the Symbols library, drawn into the box you drag with its proportions kept.

Pick a custom shape

  1. Click Shape in the options bar: it shows the current shape.
  2. Find one: type in Search, or narrow it by category.
  3. Click a tile (or use the arrow keys and Enter). Esc, or a click elsewhere, closes it as it was.
  • It's the Symbols library's current shape: clicking a tile in the Libraries window's Symbols tab picks it too (in its Library), and the window marks the one you picked here.
  • Custom… opens the Libraries window's Symbols, to save, rename or delete shapes.

Draw at an exact size

Click without dragging (with any Shape tool but Line) for Photoshop's Create box:

  • Width and Height, in the document's units.
  • Corner radius (rectangles), or Sides and Star ratio (polygons).
  • From centre (where you clicked): off, the click is the top-left corner.

Good to know

  • Shift+U steps through the group. R, O and L still pick the rectangle, ellipse and line.
  • A polygon or star stays live: Properties changes its sides and star ratio later, until you edit its points by hand.
  • Properties turns arrowheads on or off for any selected line or open path.
  • Arrowheads are one shared SVG marker drawn in each line's own stroke colour (context-stroke), sized by its stroke width.

Pencil

Draw freehand lines, smoothed as you go.

  1. Pick the Pencil.
  2. Set Smoothing in the options bar (0 to 10; 4 to start with). Higher gives smoother, simpler curves.
  3. Drag on the canvas to draw.

Good to know

  • The stroke settings in the options bar (Stroke options) apply to what you draw.
  • How it works: the line you draw is simplified (RDP) and then fitted with curves (Catmull-Rom → Bézier).

Pen

Draw precise paths, point by point, with straight lines and smooth curves.

  1. Pick the Pen.
  2. Click for a corner point, or drag for a smooth point with curve handles.
  3. Carry on clicking or dragging. Shift snaps to 45°, and Backspace removes the last point.
  4. Finish: click the first point to close the shape, or press Enter or double-click to leave it open. Esc also ends it.

Good to know

  • To change the path afterwards, use Edit points.

Free Transform and Edit → Transform

Scale, rotate and skew the selection by hand or by exact numbers, as in Photoshop.

  1. Select what to change and choose Edit → Free Transform (Alt+T).
  2. Drag a corner to scale, or the top knob to rotate. Or type exact X, Y, W and H (with the proportion lock), an angle, and horizontal (H) or vertical (V) skew in the options bar.
  3. Press Enter or click ✓ to commit. Esc or ✕ cancels the whole session.

Edit → Transform

  • Scale, Rotate and Skew open the same session with the handles set to that job: corners and edges only scale, any handle rotates, or edge handles slide along their edge to skew. Shift snaps angles to 15°.
  • Rotate 180°, Rotate 90° Clockwise, Rotate 90° Counter Clockwise, Flip Horizontal and Flip Vertical each apply in one step, about the selection's centre.
  • Again (Alt+Shift+T) repeats the last transform about the selection's current centre.
  • Again with Copy (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T) duplicates first, so a 30° rotation repeated 11 times makes a ring of 12.

Good to know

  • Browsers keep Ctrl+T and Ctrl+Shift+T for their tabs, so these shortcuts use Alt.
  • Distort, Perspective and Warp aren't included: SVG transforms can only make straight-line (affine) changes.

Align and distribute

Line objects up with each other, or space them out evenly.

  1. Select the objects with the Move tool.
  2. Click an align or distribute button on the Move tool's options bar, or choose Layer → Align or Layer → Distribute.

Options

  • Align: Left Edges, Horizontal Centres or Right Edges; Top Edges, Vertical Centres or Bottom Edges. Objects align to the selection's bounds.
  • Distribute (horizontally or vertically): spaces three or more objects with equal gaps, leaving the outermost two where they are.

Good to know

  • With one object selected, it aligns to the artboard instead, as in Photoshop.

Eyedropper

Copy a style or a colour from something already in the drawing.

  1. Pick the Eyedropper (I).
  2. Choose what it samples in the options bar: Style or Colour.
  3. Click the shape or the colour you want.

Options

  • Style: copies a shape's fill, stroke, alpha, stroke width and opacity into the current settings, and applies them to anything selected.
  • Colour: takes the exact pixel you click, including blended transparency and placed images, into the active paint. A ring around the cursor previews the colour.

Tips

  • Alt-click sends the colour to the other paint (fill or stroke).
  • In Chromium browsers, the eyedropper button on the Color panel picks a colour from anywhere on the screen.

Edit points

Reshape a path, or a basic shape, by moving its points and curve handles.

  1. Pick Edit Points (A), or double-click a shape with the Move tool.
  2. Click the shape, then drag its points and Bézier handles. The arrow keys nudge picked points.
  3. Press Esc, or pick another tool, when you're done.

Picking points

  • Shift-click points to pick several, or drag round them.
  • Choose what a drag picks with from the Edit Points button's flyout (as with the Shape tools), or step through them with Shift+A: Rectangle Select, Ellipse Select (an oval) or Lasso Select (freeform).
  • As in Photoshop, a drag begun with Shift adds to what's picked, and one begun with Alt takes points away. Alt pressed during a drag grows a rectangle or oval from its centre.

Changing points

  • Double-click a segment to add a point.
  • Double-click a point to switch it between corner and smooth (or use Corner and Smooth in the options bar).
  • Delete (Del) removes the picked points.
  • Close / open adds or removes the closing segment.
  • Smooth points keep their handles in line. Alt-drag a handle to break one.

Good to know

  • Works on paths with any command (arcs included) and on rectangles, ellipses, circles, lines, polylines and polygons.
  • A basic shape turns into a <path> only once you change it.

Fill rule and path direction

Decide which parts of a path that crosses itself, or holds other loops, are filled and which are holes.

  1. Select a path, polygon or polyline.
  2. In Properties, set Fill rule to Non-zero or Even-odd, or click Reverse to run the outline the other way.

The same commands are in Object → Path: Non-Zero Fill Rule, Even-Odd Fill Rule and Reverse Direction.

Options

  • Non-zero (SVG's default): fills an area unless the outline's directions around it cancel out.
  • Even-odd: makes every nested loop a hole, whichever way it runs.
  • Reverse (Reverse Path Direction): runs the selected paths, polygons, polylines and lines the other way. Under non-zero, a loop running against its outer shape is a hole.

Good to know

  • The fill rule is set on each selected shape, inside groups too, and saved as fill-rule (nothing for non-zero, unless a group or style above would make it even-odd).
  • Reversing also flips where text on the path starts and which way dashes and markers run. A closed path keeps its starting point.
  • Reversing turns rectangles, circles and ellipses into paths (a live rectangle's corners stop being editable as corners).

Animate

Make a layer or group fade, slide, spin, pulse, draw itself on and more, in the saved SVG.

  1. Select one layer or group and open the Animation tab.
  2. Choose a preset from Add animation….
  3. Click its row and set its options below the list.
  4. Click ▶ Play (or View → Play Animations) to preview the whole drawing. Esc, a click on the canvas or any edit stops it.

Presets

  • Entrances: Fade in, Slide in, Pop in, Zoom in, Drop in (falls in and bounces to rest), Back in (slides in, overshoots and settles), Roll in, Flip in (turns into view), Wipe in (uncovered from a side), Iris in (uncovered from the middle out) and Blur in (comes into focus). Run any of them in Reverse to take the layer away the same way.
  • Exits: Fade out, Slide out, Zoom out, Hinge (swings on its top-left corner, then drops away).
  • Loops: Spin, Pulse, Bounce, Shake, Float, Blink, Swing (back and forth about a point, like a hanging sign), Heartbeat (a double pulse), Jello (a wobble that settles), Flip (turned over like a card, and back), Glow pulse (a coloured glow round it that comes and goes), Shine (a highlight sweeping across it, as on a button), Rubber band (squashes and stretches), Tada (grows with a wiggle), Head shake (a small shake that turns), Wobble (sways side to side), Breathe (a slow fade down and up), Ripple (rings spreading out from under it and fading, one after another; Grow to sets how far, Ring width and Ring colour their look) and Flipbook (a group's layers shown one at a time, bottom first, as the frames of a flipbook or a loading spinner; the length is the whole round, and a set number of times ends on the last frame).
  • Motion: Move along path (see Move along path) and Morph (see Morph).
  • Line effects: Draw on, Draw off, Dash march, and Stroke pulse (the outline grows thicker and back; Grow to sets how thick, as a percentage of its width).
  • Colour: Colour cycle; Gradient flow (bands of its own colour and a Second colour moving across it, the way Angle points); Pattern scroll (stripes of the Stripe colour, Stripe width wide, sliding over it at the Angle).
  • Text: Typewriter: the letters appear one by one over the length. Run backwards, they go one by one.

Settings

  • Length and Delay, in seconds.
  • Times, or Forever.
  • Start after the one above: chains it to the end of the previous one (after its first run, if that one loops forever), with its delay counted from there. An entrance, a loop and an exit can then follow one another without adding up delays.
  • Run: Normal, Reverse or Back and forth.
  • Ease: Linear, Ease, Ease in, Ease out or Ease in-out.
  • Each preset's own options, such as the slide or wipe side and distance, turns, how far to grow, the colour to cycle to, the angle and point a Swing turns about, which way a Flip turns, how blurred Blur in starts, or a Glow pulse's size and colour.
  • Stagger (a group, or a text layer's letters): see Stagger.

Several on one layer

  • A layer can have several animations. They play together, each after its own delay.
  • Drag a row's ⠿ grip, or press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓, to reorder them. When two move or scale the layer, they combine in list order.

In the file

  • Animations are kept as settings on the layer (data-sc-anim) and written out as SVG animation (SMIL: <animate>, <animateTransform>, <set>) only when the drawing is saved. Editing and undo always see the shapes at rest.
  • Moves, spins and scales are additive, so they happen about the layer's own centre, on top of its transform.
  • SMIL plays in every current browser, including SVG shown in an <img> tag. Each animation adds about 150–300 bytes.
  • Export Clean SVG keeps the animation and rounds its coordinates like the rest. PNG, app icon and favicon exports use the still drawing.
  • Wipe in, Iris in, Blur in, Glow pulse, Shine, Ripple, Gradient flow and Pattern scroll need a clip, filter, mask or paint of their own: the saved file wraps the layer in a group that carries it (Shine's highlight, Ripple's rings, and the gradient or stripes, masked by the layer, go in that group too). Reopened in SVGCraft, the group is taken off again; a file from Export Clean SVG reopens with it as a group of its own, and those animations left out.
  • Reopening a saved file rebuilds the animations from their settings.

Animations from other files

When you open, import or paste an SVG with its own SMIL animations, each one that does what a preset does becomes that preset on its layer, ready to edit and play:

  • A rotation about the layer's centre becomes Spin; opacity from 0 to 1 or back becomes Fade in or Fade out; a fill going to another colour becomes Colour cycle; a motion along a path (<animateMotion>) becomes Move along path, its path a new "Motion path" layer; and so on for every preset, with its length, delay, repeats, direction and ease.
  • A file saved by Export Clean SVG (which drops SVGCraft's settings) comes back with the animations it had.
  • A move about another resting place (bars bobbing from 5 below to 5 above) becomes the preset that moves that way (here Float, 10 up and back), with the layer moved to where the move starts.
  • What no preset does is left out, and a message says how many; its More info button says which and why (see Animations left out). Among them: a motion at a fixed angle, an animation that starts on another animation's end, one inside a symbol, and CSS @keyframes.
  • An animation that replaces a layer's own transform (SMIL's default) is only kept when the layer has none, since a preset adds to it.

Animations left out

See exactly which of a file's animations SVGCraft couldn't keep, and why, so you can fix the file or rebuild them with presets.

  1. Open the file. If some animations can't be kept, a warning says how many.
  2. Click More info in the warning → the report lists each one.

What it shows

  • Where: the layer it was on, or the part of the file (a <style> block, the whole drawing, an element that isn't there).
  • The markup: the animation element as it was in the file.
  • Why: the reason it was left out: its timing can't be set in SVGCraft, it animates something no preset does, it's a CSS animation, it's inside a symbol…
  • Nearest preset: when a preset nearly matched, which one and how it differs (its values, timing or turning point), so you can add that preset and adjust it.

Settings

  • Copy report → the whole report as text, to paste into a bug report or a note.

Good to know

  • What's left out isn't in the drawing any more: saving won't write it. Reopen the original file to get it back.

When an animation starts

Start an animation on a click or when the pointer is over a layer, after another layer's animations, or with a pause between its runs.

  1. Select the layer, open the Animation tab and click the animation's row.
  2. Choose under Start:
    • When the file opens (after its Delay).
    • On click: when the layer is clicked, or the one chosen under Clicking, such as a button.
    • On hover: when the pointer is over it (or the one chosen under Pointing at). One that runs Forever stops when the pointer leaves.
    • After another layer: when the animations of the layer chosen under After have finished (their first run, for one that runs forever).
  3. For a loop, set Pause to wait that long between one run and the next.

Good to know

  • Delay counts from the start you chose: a click, the end of the other layer's animations, or the file opening.
  • An entrance that waits for a click stays hidden until then.
  • Clicks and the pointer work where the SVG is a page of its own or part of one (opened directly, inline, or in an <object> or <iframe>). An <img> tag never passes them on, so there it waits for ever.
  • ▶ Play shows them as if the click had happened.
  • In the file they're SMIL begin times such as begin="button.click+0.5s", so the layer clicked gets an id. A pause makes each run longer, holding its last frame to the end.

Pivot

Choose the point an animation turns or grows about, as you'd move the reference point in Photoshop's Free Transform: a clock hand turning about its end, a sign swinging from its hook, a badge growing out of a corner.

  1. Select the layer and open the Animation tab.
  2. Pick an animation that turns or grows: Spin, Pulse, Swing, Heartbeat, Pop in, Zoom in or out, Roll in, Flip in, Flip, Jello, Rubber band, Tada, Head shake or Wobble.
  3. Drag the ⊕ on the canvas to where it should turn. Near the layer's corners, edge middles and centre it snaps to them.

Settings

  • Pivot: where the ⊕ is, across and down the layer's box, in % (50 %, 50 % is the centre). Type a value to place it exactly; it can go outside the layer too.
  • ↺ next to it, or double-click the ⊕ → back to the centre.
  • Swing from picks a side of the layer; once you drag the ⊕ elsewhere it reads Custom.

Good to know

  • The ⊕ shows while the Animation tab is open, for the animation chosen in its list. Each animation on a layer has its own pivot.
  • The pivot is kept relative to the layer, so moving or resizing the layer takes it along. On a rotated layer, across and down follow the layer's own sides.
  • Files that turn or grow a layer about a point of their own (say rotate(0 50 50) to rotate(360 50 50)) open as that animation with its pivot there, ready to edit.

Stagger

Run one animation on a group's layers, or a text's letters, one after another: paints popping in in turn, letters fading in.

  1. Select the group (or the text layer) and open the Animation tab.
  2. Add an animation, as for one layer.
  3. Set Stagger to the time between one starting and the next.

Good to know

  • The group's layers go from the bottom of the Layers panel to the top, each after the stagger, with the animation's own delay before the first.
  • Each layer runs it about its own centre, as if you'd added it to each.
  • Letters work with Fade in, Fade out, Blink and Colour cycle. Spaces are skipped. For letters appearing at a steady pace, use the Typewriter preset instead.
  • A Stagger of 0 runs it on the group (or text) as a whole.
  • In the file, each layer (or letter) gets its own SMIL. Saved by SVGCraft, it reopens as the one animation on the group; Export Clean SVG reopens as an animation on each layer.

Move along path

Send a layer along a line you draw: a car along a road, a plane along its flight path.

  1. Draw the route with the Pen or Pencil, or use any shape (a rectangle, circle, ellipse, line or polygon). It must be above the layer that moves.
  2. Select the layer, then Shift-click the route, and open the Animation tab.
  3. Choose Add animation… → Move along path.
  4. Click ▶ Play: the layer's centre travels the route from its start to its end, then stays there.

Settings

  • Path: the layer it follows. Pick another shape here to change the route.
  • Orient to path: the layer turns to face the way it's going, like a car on a road. It points along the route the way it's drawn facing (its own rightward direction leads).
  • Hide the path when saved: the route is left out of sight in the saved file, so only the moving layer shows. It stays visible while you edit, and comes back when you reopen the file.
  • Length, Delay, Times, Run and Ease work as for every animation. Reverse runs from the end of the route to its start; Back and forth goes there and back.

Good to know

  • Reshape or move the route and the animation follows: it's linked, not copied. Delete it and the animation stops, and its Path reads "— gone —" until you pick another.
  • A closed shape (a circle, a rectangle) makes a loop: set Forever for something that keeps circling.
  • It combines with the other animations: a layer can Pulse or Spin while it travels.
  • In the file it's an <animateMotion> along the route (as seen from the layer), plus a fixed shift that puts the layer's centre on the line.

Morph

Turn one shape into another: a play icon into a pause icon, a circle into a star, a blob that wobbles between two outlines.

  1. Draw the shape it should become, above the layer that changes.
  2. Select the layer, then Shift-click that shape, and open the Animation tab.
  3. Choose Add animation… → Morph. A rectangle, circle, ellipse, line or polygon becomes a path (only a path can change its outline).
  4. Click ▶ Play: the outline turns into the other shape, where that shape is, and stays.

Settings

  • Into: the shape it becomes. Pick another here.
  • Hide that shape when saved: the target is left out of sight in the saved file, so only the morphing layer shows. It stays visible while you edit, and comes back when you reopen the file.
  • Run: Back and forth turns it into the other shape and back, and with Forever keeps doing so; Reverse starts as the other shape.

Good to know

  • Any two outlines work. Each is turned into curves; parts pair up biggest with biggest, the one with more points sets how many both have, and the start is chosen to keep the change smooth. A part with no partner (a hole that the other shape doesn't have) grows from or shrinks to a point.
  • Only the outline changes. The fill and stroke stay the layer's own (add Colour cycle to change the colour as well).
  • Reshape the target and the morph follows: it's linked, not copied.
  • In the file it's an <animate> of the path's d. Opening a file with one gives a Morph, with the outline it ends on as a "Morph target" layer.

Zoom and pan

Get close to the detail, or step back to see the whole drawing.

  • Zoom tool (Z): click to zoom in one step (50%, 66.7%, 100%, 200%, 300% …). Alt-click, or choose the options bar's Zoom Out button, to step out.
  • Drag with the Zoom tool: with Scrubby Zoom on, drag right to zoom in and left to zoom out, centred where you pressed. With it off, drag a box to fill the window with that area.
  • 100%, Fit Screen and Fill Screen are on the Zoom and Hand tools' options bar. Double-click the Zoom tool for 100%.
  • View menu: Zoom In (+), Zoom Out (−), Fit on Screen (0) and 100% (1).
  • Ctrl/⌘ + wheel, or a pinch, zooms the canvas.
  • Pan: scroll the wheel (Shift+wheel goes sideways), drag with the Hand tool, or hold Space and drag with any tool.

The page itself doesn't zoom

  • The browser's zoom keys (Ctrl/⌘ + =, − and 0) zoom the canvas instead, like Photoshop's.
  • Ctrl/⌘ + wheel or a pinch only ever zooms the canvas, never the panels.
  • On phones and tablets the page can't be pinched or double-tapped bigger.

Pixel grid and Snap to Pixel

Keep icons and pixel art crisp, with edges on whole pixels.

  1. Turn on View → Pixel Grid and View → Snap to Pixel (or the Pixel grid and Snap to pixel boxes under Document in Properties).
  2. Zoom to 600% or more to see the grid.
  3. Draw and move as usual: points and moved shapes land on whole pixels.

Good to know

  • The pixel grid is a 1 px grid over the artboard, shown from 600% zoom up.
  • Snapping to pixels keeps edges sharp in PNG exports and at small sizes.
  • A centred stroke of odd whole width (1, 3 px …) snaps to half pixels instead, so its edges land on whole pixels.
  • Guides and smart guides still win when they're close, and Snap to Grid wins when it's on.
  • Both settings are remembered.

Eraser

Rub out whole objects, or cut gaps in lines.

  1. Pick the Eraser.
  2. Choose Object or Cut in the options bar, and set its Size.
  3. Rub over what you want to erase.

Options

  • Object: deletes anything you rub.
  • Cut: splits stroked lines and paths where you rub, and leaves filled shapes alone.

Gradients

Fill or stroke a shape with a smooth blend of colours.

  1. Select a shape and, in the Color panel, click Fill or Stroke to make it the active paint.
  2. Set its Type to Linear or Radial (or back to Solid).
  3. Edit the stops in the gradient editor below.
  4. To set the direction on the canvas, pick the Gradient tool (G) and drag across the selection. Shift snaps to 45°, and a radial gradient drags from the centre outwards. Drag the end handles to adjust it.

The gradient editor

  • The bar: click it to add a stop, drag a stop to move it, or drag it down off the bar to remove it.
  • Each stop has a colour, Opacity and Location. The bin button deletes it.
  • Angle: the direction, in degrees.
  • Reverse (⇄) flips the stops.
  • Stretch with shape (off by default): off, stretching or skewing the shape keeps the gradient at its angle, still running across the whole shape, and a radial one stays round. On, it stretches with the shape.
  • Presets: the button beside the title shows the gradient in use (or Custom). Click it for the tiles: Colour → Transparent, plus everything in the Gradients library, which marks the same one. Picking a tile swaps in its stops and keeps the type and angle.
  • + saves the gradient to the Gradients library.
  • Custom…, in the picker, opens the Libraries window's Gradients to rename, delete, import or export them.

Tips

  • With a gradient active, clicking a swatch recolours the selected stop.
  • The Gradient tool's options bar switches between Linear and Radial for the active paint of the selection.

Good to know

  • Each shape gets its own gradient, which moves, rotates and scales with the shape. With Stretch with shape off, it's laid out in the shape's space as the page shows it (its gradientTransform undoes the shape's stretch and skew), and fitted to the shape again after every change, keeping where it sits in the shape (data-fit).
  • Duplicates split off their own copy when edited, and unused gradients are removed automatically.
  • Gradients in imported files are read, including ones that borrow stops from another gradient.

Stroke options

Set how outlines look: thickness, position, ends, corners and dashes.

  1. Select a shape, or pick a drawing tool to set the stroke for what you draw next.
  2. Set the stroke under Stroke in the Color panel, or in the drawing tool's options bar. Both show whatever other panel is open.

Settings

  • Width: the thickness, in px.
  • Align: Inside, Center or Outside, as in Photoshop, for closed shapes (rectangles, ellipses, polygons and closed paths).
  • Caps: butt, round or square line ends.
  • Joins: miter, round or bevel corners (in the Color panel).
  • Dashes: Solid, Dashed, Dotted or Long dash.
  • Custom dashes: opens Photoshop's dash / gap fields in the Color panel: up to three dash-and-gap pairs, in stroke widths. Imported dash patterns show up there too.

Good to know

  • Dash lengths are in multiples of the stroke width, as in Photoshop, so they keep their proportions when the width changes.
  • Dashes allow for round and square caps, which extend each dash, so dotted lines come out as round dots.
  • SVG strokes are always centred, so an aligned stroke is drawn twice as wide and the unwanted half is hidden: clipped to the shape for Inside, and painted under the fill for Outside (masked when there's no fill). The width you set stays the visible width.
  • Under a semi-transparent fill, the hidden half of an Outside stroke shows through faintly.
  • Opening a path puts its stroke back to Center.

Rounded rectangles

Round the corners of a rectangle, all together or one at a time.

  • Before drawing: set a Radius on the Rectangle tool's options bar.
  • On a selected rectangle: edit its four corners under Corner radius in Properties. The link toggle changes them all together.
  • On the canvas: drag the round handles inside the corners. Alt-drag moves a single corner, as in Photoshop's live corners.

In the file

  • Equal corners stay a plain <rect rx>.
  • Unequal corners become a path that remembers it's a rectangle, so its radii stay editable until you edit its points.

Patterns

Fill or stroke a shape with a repeating tile: stripes, dots, bricks, or a tile you make.

  1. Select a shape and make fill or stroke the active paint.
  2. Set the paint's Type to Pattern in the Color panel.
  3. Adjust it in the pattern editor: Scale, Angle, Stretch with shape, or another pattern: click the pattern's name for the library's tiles (the same ones as the Libraries window's Patterns, which marks the one in use). Custom… opens that window, to make and manage patterns.

Stretch with shape

  • Off (the default): scaling, stretching or skewing the shape leaves the tiles their size, so a bigger shape shows more of the pattern. They still move and turn with it.
  • On: the tiles grow, shrink and stretch with the shape, as if it were one picture.

Make your own

  • Select what the tile should hold and choose Edit → Define Pattern…, as in Photoshop. The tile is the size of the selection's visible box.
  • It looks the same as it does on the canvas, including transforms, gradients and clip paths.

Good to know

  • The built-ins (stripes, diagonal, dots, grid, checks, crosshatch, waves, bricks, triangles) are drawn in the paint's colour, so changing the colour re-inks them.
  • The tiles start at the shape's top-left corner.
  • As with gradients, each shape gets its own <pattern> in its own coordinates. Unless Stretch with shape is on, its patternTransform undoes the shape's scale and skew, and is kept so as the shape changes.
  • Patterns export as plain SVG.

Libraries

Make, keep and manage your own colours, gradients, patterns and symbols, and share them with other apps.

  1. Choose Window → Libraries, or Custom… in any picker (a swatch, gradient, pattern or custom shape): the window opens on that tab.
  2. Pick a tab: Swatches, Gradients, Patterns or Symbols.
  3. Manage the tiles with the bar below them.

Using them is done where you work: the Color panel's Fill and Stroke pick swatches, gradients and patterns from their own pickers, and the Custom Shape tool draws a symbol.

The tiles

  • Apply: click a tile to apply it to the active paint, or Shift-click it to apply it to the other one.
  • Add (+): adds the current colour (with its alpha), saves the active gradient, or defines a pattern from the selection. Each asks for a name.
  • Rename: double-click a tile, or use the pencil button.
  • Delete: Alt-click a tile, or use the bin button. The library isn't in the drawing's history, so the message after it has its own Undo.
  • Reset (↺): brings back the built-in set for that tab.

Swatches, Gradients and Patterns all work this way; Symbols has its own bar (see Symbols). They're saved in this browser (localStorage), like Photoshop's presets.

Good to know

  • It opens docked in a column of its own between the canvas and the panels. Drag the column's left edge (or focus it and use the arrow keys) to change its width.
  • Its title bar's float button turns it into a window you can move and size over the canvas; the same button docks it back. SVGCraft remembers which, and the column's width.
  • Esc or ✕ closes it, and it opens again on the tab you last used.

Export

Export, on any of the tabs, saves the whole library, symbols included, as one svgcraft-library.zip:

  • svgcraft-library.json: everything, for SVGCraft.
  • swatches.gpl: a palette for GIMP, Inkscape and Krita.
  • swatches.css and gradients.css: CSS custom properties (--name: #hex, --name: linear-gradient(…)).
  • gradients.svg and patterns.svg: <linearGradient>, <radialGradient> and <pattern> defs for Inkscape, Illustrator and browsers, each drawn as a labelled sample. Pattern tiles draw in currentColor, set on each <pattern>.
  • symbols.svg: an SVG sprite, one <symbol id="…"> per symbol with its credit, for <use href="symbols.svg#id"/>.
  • README.txt: what each file is.

Kinds with nothing in them are left out.

Import

Import adds a file's contents, skipping anything you already have (the same colour, gradient, tile or symbol, whatever its name). If something new has the name of one of yours, SVGCraft asks once for the whole import:

  • Keep both (the default): the imported one becomes "Sky 2".
  • Replace mine: yours keeps its name and place and takes the new definition.
  • Skip them.

It reads:

  • the exported zip (from its svgcraft-library.json);
  • a zip of palettes, gradients and SVGs without one (deflated or not, in folders or not);
  • a JSON library;
  • a GIMP palette (including GIMP 3's alpha) or a GIMP gradient (.ggr);
  • any SVG, taking its gradients (shared stops included), patterns and symbols. Symbols from an SVG go in a category named after the file.

Good to know

  • Browser storage belongs to one browser on one machine and is lost if you clear the site's data, so export to keep a copy.
  • Pattern tiles and symbols from a file are sanitised like imported drawings.

Colours

Set the fill and stroke colours of what you draw or have selected, and how see-through they are.

  1. Click Fill or Stroke in the Color panel (or the fill and stroke chips at the bottom of the toolbar) to make it the active paint.
  2. Tick On to paint it, or untick it for none.
  3. Click the paint's swatch for the colour picker, type a hex code, or pick a swatch with the swatches button beside the hex code (its Custom… opens the Libraries window's Swatches).
  4. For a gradient or a pattern, set the paint's Type: its editor opens inside that paint's section, under the Type.

Fill and Stroke

  • Each folds to its first row with the arrow at its left, to save room; SVGCraft remembers which you folded.
  • The stroke's width, alignment, caps, joins and dashes sit under Stroke.

Transparency

  • Alpha, under Fill and under Stroke: how see-through each paint is.
  • Opacity, in the Layers panel: how see-through the whole object is.
  • The three are separate, and the artboard's checkerboard shows the result.

Shortcuts

  • X (or Edit → Swap Fill and Stroke) swaps fill and stroke.
  • Shift-click a swatch to apply it to the other paint.

Selecting, moving and arranging

Pick objects, then move, resize, rotate, group and stack them.

  • Select: click with the Move tool. Shift-click adds, and dragging on empty canvas draws a marquee. Select → All (Ctrl+A), Deselect (Ctrl+D) and Inverse (Shift+F7).
  • Move: drag the selection, or nudge it with the arrow keys (Shift moves 10 times as far).
  • Resize and rotate: drag the handles. Shift keeps the ratio, and Alt scales from the centre. Drag the knob above to rotate.
  • Flip: the flip buttons on the options bar, or Object → Flip Horizontal / Flip Vertical.
  • Group (Ctrl+G) and Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G).
  • Stacking order: Layer → Arrange: Bring to Front (Ctrl+Shift+]), Bring Forward (Ctrl+]), Send Backward (Ctrl+[) and Send to Back (Ctrl+Shift+[).
  • Duplicate: Layer → Duplicate Layer.
  • Undo and redo: Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z.

More on this

  • Selecting in the Layers panel: Select layers and the Select menu.
  • Group and ungroup, and Reorder, copy and delete in the Layers panel.
  • Show, hide and lock layers.
  • The grid and snapping: Rulers, guides and smart guides.
  • Document size: Units and page size.
  • Zoom and pan.

Type

Set headlines, labels and blocks of text with the Type tool (T), which works like Photoshop's. Text stays live and editable, and saves as ordinary SVG text.

Add text

Type a single line, or a block that wraps inside a box.

  1. Pick the Type tool (T).
  2. Click where the text should start for point text, which grows as you type. Or drag a box for paragraph text, which wraps inside the box.
  3. Type. Enter starts a new line.
  4. Press Ctrl/⌘+Enter, or click away, to finish. Esc cancels.

The options bar

  • Font family: opens the font picker.
  • Style: the weights and italics the font has.
  • Size, in px. Drag the icon to adjust it.
  • Alignment: left, centre or right.
  • Character and Paragraph panels (¶): opens the Character and Paragraph panels.

Edit text on the canvas

Change the words of a text layer right where it sits.

  • Click the text with the Type tool, or double-click it with Move → it opens for editing on the canvas.
  • It's shown in its own font, size, colour and rotation while you type.
  • Ctrl/⌘+Enter or clicking away finishes; Esc cancels.

Good to know

  • Undo while typing covers the typing itself. Character-style changes are undone as part of the finished edit.

Choose a font

Find a font and apply it, from your system fonts or the whole Google Fonts catalogue.

  1. Select a text layer (or the characters you're editing).
  2. Click the font name in the options bar or the Character panel.
  3. Type to search, or pick a category, then click a font.

The picker

  • Search fonts: looks through every family. Names that start with what you typed come first, then names with a word that does, then names that contain it.
  • Popular (where it opens): web-safe system fonts and about 40 popular Google Fonts.
  • All: system fonts, the whole Google Fonts catalogue (about 1,900 families) and any installed fonts.
  • Sans, Serif, Display, Script, Mono: one Google Fonts category.
  • Show fonts installed on this computer… (Chromium browsers): adds your own fonts through the browser's Local Font Access permission.

Good to know

  • Each name is shown in its own face. It loads a tiny preview of itself as it scrolls into view.
  • Long lists show their first 150 names and narrow as you type.
  • The Style menu only offers the weights and italics the font really has.
  • A drawing opened from elsewhere in any Google family loads that family.
  • The catalogue (google-fonts.js, 13 KB compressed) is regenerated with scripts/gen-google-fonts.mjs.

Style individual characters

Give some characters their own font, size or colour, as in Photoshop.

  1. Edit the text (click it with the Type tool).
  2. Select characters: drag, double-click a word, or Shift+arrows.
  3. Change the font, style, size, tracking, baseline shift, caps, super/subscript, underline, strikethrough or Fill colour. Only those characters change.

Good to know

  • The options bar, Character panel, font picker and colour controls all keep the edit open. They show the settings of the characters under the caret.
  • With nothing selected while editing, a change applies to the whole layer.
  • Applying a setting to a selected layer when you're not editing styles the whole layer and clears that setting from its characters, as in Photoshop.
  • Auto leading is 120% of the largest size on each line. Paragraph text wraps by the real width of every run.

Character panel

Set the font and spacing of a text layer, or of the characters you've selected.

  • Open it from Type → Character Panel, the Character tab, or the ¶ button in the Type options bar.
  • Select a text layer → changes apply to the whole layer. While editing → they apply to the selected characters.

Settings

  • Font family and Style: as in the options bar.
  • Size, in px.
  • Lead (leading, line spacing): leave it empty for Auto, 120% of the size.
  • Track (tracking): in thousandths of an em, as in Photoshop.
  • Shift (baseline shift), in px.
  • Toggles: All Caps, Small Caps, Superscript, Subscript, Underline and Strikethrough.
  • Colour comes from the Fill paint.

Paragraph panel

Set how lines line up and how wide a text box is, or switch between point and paragraph text.

  • Open it from Type → Paragraph Panel or the Paragraph tab.
  • Select a text layer, then change its settings.

Settings

  • Alignment: left, centre or right.
  • Box width: the width of a paragraph text box, in px.
  • Convert to Paragraph Text / Convert to Point Text: switches the kind of text. Also on Type → Convert Point / Paragraph Text.

Text in the saved file

Your text and its fonts go with the file, so it looks the same elsewhere.

  • Export an SVG → it links the Google Fonts it uses, so it renders the same in any browser.
  • Export a PNG → the fonts are downloaded and embedded in the image, because an SVG drawn into an image isn't allowed to fetch fonts.
  • Installed (local) fonts only look right on computers that have them.
  • Need shapes instead of text? Type → Create Outlines (Ctrl+Shift+O) turns text into shapes (see Create Outlines).

Good to know

  • No Warp Text yet.
  • A text layer is ordinary SVG text: one <tspan> per line and a nested <tspan> per styled run, with the settings in standard attributes. The type details survive export and import, and other editors can read the file.

Text on a path

Set text along a curve, a circle or any shape's outline, like Illustrator's Type on a Path. The text stays live: edit the path and the text follows.

Put text on a path

Run a line of text along a path or round a shape.

  1. Select one text layer and one path or shape (a path, rectangle, ellipse, circle, polygon, polyline or line): Shift-click both.
  2. Choose Type → Text on Path, or click Put Text on Path in the Properties panel.

Good to know

  • The text's lines are joined into one, with a space where each line break was.
  • Its fonts, per-character styles, fill, effects, blend mode, lock and name stay.
  • The path layer stays where it is and keeps its own paint. Give it no stroke, or hide it, if you only want the text.
  • On a closed shape the text starts where the shape does: an ellipse's or circle's right-hand point, a rectangle's top-left corner.

Adjust text on a path

Slide the text along its path, flip it, reshape the path or change the words.

  • Select the text-on-path layer → the Properties panel shows its options.
  • Move, rotate, scale or point-edit the path layer, or the group it's in → the text re-flows along it straight away.
  • Move the text layer on its own → it stays on the path, because the text follows the path.
  • Double-click the text with Move, or click it with the Type tool → edit the words. It's edited as one straight line where it starts on the path; Enter or clicking away finishes.

Options

  • Start: where the text starts along the path, in percent.
  • Align: the text starts at, is centred on, or ends at that point. Picking one also sets Start to 0, 50 or 100%.
  • Flip: puts the text on the other side of the path, running the other way.

Good to know

  • Character panel and options-bar changes (font, size, tracking, colour, caps…) apply to the whole text and keep it on the path.
  • Paragraph settings that need lines (box width, Convert to Paragraph Text) don't apply.

Release text from a path

Turn text on a path back into ordinary text.

  1. Select the text-on-path layer.
  2. Choose Type → Release Text on Path, or click Release Text on Path in the Properties panel.

It becomes one line of point text, placed where it started on the path.

If the path layer is deleted

  • The text keeps the last shape it ran along and stays where it was, so nothing jumps or disappears. The Properties panel says its path layer is gone.
  • Release it to make it ordinary text again.

How text on a path is saved

Text on a path is standard SVG, so other browsers and editors show it.

  • The text is a standard <text> with a <textPath> pointing at a copy of the path's shape in <defs>. SVG ignores the referenced path's own transform, so the copy is kept in the text's coordinates.
  • data-sc-textpath on the text names the path layer's id. The path layer gets an id if it had none.
  • The link survives Save → reopen, Import and paste (ids that clash are renamed and the link follows), undo and Duplicate. Duplicating the text with its path links the copy to the copied path.

Layers

The Layers panel works like Photoshop's. Every shape is a layer, groups are folders, and you select, stack, hide, lock, blend and style layers from it.

Layer rows and folders

Use the Layers panel to see what your drawing is made of and pick out any part of it.

  • One row per layer. Every shape is a layer, including the shapes inside a group.
  • Groups are folders. Click a folder's arrow to expand or collapse it. Each level is indented.
  • Imported SVGs arrive as a folder named after the file, with one layer per shape inside it.

With the keyboard

Tab to the list (it lands on the selected row), then:

  • ↑ ↓ (Home, End): select the row above or below; Shift adds it.
  • Alt+↑ / Alt+↓: move the layer up or down the stack.
  • F2 or Enter: rename it.
  • → / ←: open or fold a folder.
  • Shift+F10 (or the menu key): its right-click menu.

Good to know

  • Everything works at any depth. Move, scale, rotate, flip, nudge, align, distribute, duplicate, copy, colours, the eraser and point editing all work on a layer inside a group, so you never have to ungroup first.
  • Every row has a preview, groups (of what's in them) and hidden layers too.
  • Previews are drawn just after the list: the rows in view first, the rest while the browser is idle. So a long list appears at once.

Select layers

Pick the layers you want to work on.

  • Click a row to select it.
  • Ctrl/⌘-click a row to add it to the selection, or remove it.
  • Shift-click a row to select the run of rows from the last one you clicked.

A group and a layer inside it are never selected together.

Group and ungroup

Put layers in a folder so they move, hide and style together.

  1. Select the layers.
  2. Press Ctrl+G, choose Layer → Group Layers, or click the folder button at the bottom of the panel.

The new group (Group 1, Group 2 …) goes where the frontmost of the layers was. With nothing selected, you get an empty group.

To take a group apart again, select it and choose Layer → Ungroup Layers (Ctrl+Shift+G).

Reorder, copy and delete

Change what's in front, or copy and delete layers, by dragging their rows.

  • Reorder: drag a row. Drop on the top half of a row to put the layer in front of it, or on the bottom half to put it behind.
  • Into a group: drop on the middle of a folder.
  • To the back: drop on the empty space at the bottom of the list.
  • Copy in place: drop rows on the New button (the plus square) at the bottom of the panel, as in Photoshop. The copies go just above the originals.
  • Delete: drop rows on the bin.

Dragging a selected row moves the whole selection.

Good to know

  • Clicking New duplicates the selection, a little offset.
  • Layers never move on screen when they change groups. Paint they inherited from their old group (such as an icon's fill="none") goes with them.

Show, hide and lock

Hide layers you're not working on, and lock the ones you don't want to change by accident.

  • Hide or show: click a row's eye.
  • Show just one layer: Alt-click its eye, as in Photoshop. Every other layer hides (the groups it's in stay shown). Alt-click it again and the others come back as they were. Right-clicking the eye offers Hide All Other Layers and Show All Other Layers too.
  • Lock: select layers and click a Lock button at the top of the panel, or use Layer → Lock Position / Lock All.
  • Unlock: click the padlock on the row, or choose Layer → Unlock.

Lock options

  • Lock position: stops the layer moving, scaling, rotating, flipping, nudging and aligning.
  • Lock all: stops every change: paint, styles, blend mode, point and text edits, deleting and erasing.

Good to know

  • Locked layers can still be selected.
  • A lock on a group covers everything in it.

Right-click a layer

Right-click a row in the Layers panel for what you can do with the layer.

  • The row: it's selected (unless it's already in the selection), and the menu offers Rename Layer…, Duplicate, Delete, Arrange, Group, Clipping Mask, Combine Shapes, symbols, Layer Style, Copy / Paste / Clear Layer Style, Lock, Merge Down, Merge Visible and Copy as SVG.
