  • The eye: Hide (or Show) This Layer, and Hide All Other Layers, which leaves only this one showing (the groups it's in stay shown). Once the others are hidden, the same item reads Show All Other Layers.

Good to know

  • As on the canvas, the menu lists only what can run now.

Rename a layer

Give layers names you'll recognise.

  1. Double-click the layer's name.
  2. Type the new name.
  3. Press Enter to save, or Esc to cancel.

An empty name goes back to the automatic one.

Good to know

  • Names are saved as data-name, which Illustrator uses too.
  • Inkscape layer labels are read on import.

Blend mode and opacity

Make a layer see-through, or mix it with the layers below.

  1. Select the layer or group.
  2. Pick a blend mode from the menu at the top of the panel.
  3. Type an Opacity, or drag its label.

Blend modes

  • Normal, Darken, Multiply, Color Burn, Lighten, Screen, Color Dodge, Overlay, Soft Light, Hard Light, Difference, Exclusion, Hue, Saturation, Color and Luminosity, as in Photoshop.
  • Pass Through (groups only): the group's layers blend with whatever is below the group. A new group starts out on Pass Through.

Good to know

  • Blend mode and opacity belong to a layer, and a group is a layer: on a group they apply to the group as a whole.
  • Setting a group to Normal isolates it, so its layers blend only with each other. Any other mode isolates it too.
  • They're saved as the layer's CSS (mix-blend-mode, isolation), which browsers apply to exported SVGs too.

Merge layers

Turn several layers into one, as in Photoshop, but the result stays vector and nothing on screen changes.

  1. Select what to merge.
  2. Choose Layer → Merge Down (Ctrl+E). The menu item names what it will do.

What gets merged

  • Merge Down: one layer selected merges it into the one below, keeping the lower one's name.
  • Merge Layers: several layers selected merge into one.
  • Merge Group: a selected group's contents merge into one.
  • Merge Visible (Ctrl+Shift+E): merges every visible layer and leaves hidden ones alone.

Good to know

  • Shapes alike in every way that shows become one path. Side by side, their outlines are joined; overlapping, they're united, which looks the same only for opaque fills with no stroke.
  • Anything else becomes one group, with the alike shapes in it joined the same way: three red shapes and a blue one become a group of one red path and the blue shape.
  • A shape is only joined to one lower down when nothing between them overlaps it, so what's on top stays on top. Shapes that can't join keep their own layers in the group.

Group by Colour

Tidy a drawing, an imported one say, into one group per colour.

  1. Choose Layer → Group by Colour….
  2. Read the warning and click Group by Colour. It asks first, because it takes every group in the drawing apart and reorders the layers.

Each group is named after its colour or its swatch. One undo puts everything back.

Good to know

  • Shapes with no fill are grouped by stroke. Gradients and patterns are grouped by which one they use.
  • The drawing looks the same afterwards. A layer only joins its colour's group when nothing of another colour that overlaps it is stacked in between. Otherwise its colour gets a second group ("Red 2").
  • Groups whose look depends on being a group stay whole and are grouped as one layer: a clipping mask, layer style, filter, blend mode, opacity below 100% or an animation. So do locked groups. They're named "Mixed" if they hold more than one colour.

Layer via Copy / Cut

Put the selected part of a layer on a new layer above it, as in Photoshop.

  1. Select layers, or pick points with Edit Points.
  2. Choose Layer → New → Layer via Copy (Ctrl+J) or Layer via Cut (Alt+Shift+J).

The new layer is selected with the Move tool.

With layers selected

  • Layer via Copy copies them in place. (Duplicate Layer offsets its copy by 10 px so it shows.)
  • Layer via Cut lifts shapes picked inside a group (Auto-Select: Layer) out onto layers of their own, just above the group and looking the same.

With points picked

  • The segments between the points go to a new path, drawn like the original.
  • Layer via Copy leaves the original whole.
  • Layer via Cut takes them out, and the original splits where they were.

Layer Style (fx)

Add shadows, glows, an overlay or a blur to a layer, as with Photoshop's Layer Style dialog.

  1. Select the layer.
  2. Open the dialog: click the fx button at the bottom of the Layers panel, choose Layer → Layer Style…, or double-click the layer's fx badge. Double-clicking a row anywhere but its name (the thumbnail, or the space after the name) opens it too.
  3. Tick an effect on the left to turn it on, or click its name to turn it on and edit it.
  4. Watch the canvas preview the changes as you edit. Untick Preview to compare.
  5. Click OK to keep them. Cancel or Esc puts everything back.

To remove all the effects, choose Layer → Clear Layer Style.

To give other layers the same look, select the styled layer and choose Layer → Copy Layer Style, then select the others and choose Layer → Paste Layer Style. It copies the effects, the blend mode and the opacity. Both are in the layer's right-click menu too.

Effects

  • Drop Shadow and Inner Shadow: colour, opacity, angle, distance, spread / choke and size.
  • Outer Glow and Inner Glow: colour, opacity, spread / choke and size.
  • Color Overlay: colour and opacity.
  • Gaussian Blur: radius.
  • Blending Options: blend mode and opacity.

Good to know

  • Angles, distances and sizes are in document pixels, as in Photoshop, so a rotated or scaled layer still casts its shadow the same way.
  • Each layer gets its own SVG <filter>, which follows the layer as it changes and is exported with it.

Tooltips

Hover over any button to find out what it does.

  • Hover a button for its tooltip. Tools also show a one-line description of what they do.
  • Tab to a button to show its tip too.
  • Tap a button on a touch screen to show its tip briefly.

Tooltips float above everything, panels and menus included. One stays while the pointer is on its button (or the button has focus), and goes when you move away, click, or press a key.

Combine Shapes

Merge shapes into one path, as Photoshop and Illustrator do.

Combine selected shapes

Build a new shape out of simpler ones: a keyhole from a circle and a rectangle, a crescent from two circles.

  1. Select two or more shapes.
  2. Click one of the four buttons in the Move tool's options bar, or choose Object → Combine Shapes and a mode.

The result takes the place, name and style of the topmost shape (the backmost one for Subtract Front). It keeps its curves, so you can point-edit it straight away.

Modes

  • Unite: the outline of all the shapes together.
  • Subtract Front: the backmost shape minus everything in front of it.
  • Intersect: only the area where all the shapes overlap.
  • Exclude: the areas where an odd number of shapes overlap, so the overlaps become holes.

Good to know

  • A group counts as one shape made of everything in it.
  • Rotated, scaled and nested layers combine where they are on screen.
  • Text and images are skipped, and you get a message saying so.
  • The geometry comes from paper.js, which loads the first time you combine shapes.

Clipping masks

Show art only through the outline of a shape or text, as Illustrator does. The clip stays live, so you can move the window or the art afterwards.

Make a clipping mask

Show your art only through the outline of the topmost shape.

  1. Put the shape or text that will be the window on top of the art.
  2. Select it and the layers to clip.
  3. Choose Layer → Clipping Mask → Make (Ctrl+Alt+G), or click the scissors button at the bottom of the Layers panel.

Everything selected goes into a new "Clipping group" where the clipping path was, without moving on screen. Only the art inside the clipping path's outline shows; the clipping path itself isn't painted.

Good to know

  • The topmost selected layer is the clipping path. It has to be a single shape or a text layer. Anything else (a group, an image) gets a message saying why, and nothing changes.
  • Locked layers can't be clipped.
  • The clip is saved in the file and is still live when you open it again.

Edit the clip

Change what shows through the window, without touching the art.

  • Move the window: click the clipping path's row to select it, then move, transform or point-edit it. The window changes and the art stays put.
  • Move everything: select the group and move it. Both move together.
  • Clip more art: drop another layer into the group.
  • End the clip: delete the clipping path, or drag it out of the group.

In the Layers panel the group and the clipping path are marked with scissors, and the clipping path's name is underlined.

Good to know

  • Duplicated clipping groups clip on their own.

Release a clipping mask

Turn the clip off and get the clipping path back as an ordinary shape.

  1. Select the clipping group, or any layer in it.
  2. Choose Layer → Clipping Mask → Release (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G).

The clipping path shows again with its own fill and stroke, and the layers stay grouped, the group renamed as a plain group (Group 1 …).

Good to know

  • A locked clipping group can't be released.

Create Outlines

Turn text into shapes, as Illustrator's Create Outlines and Photoshop's Convert to Shape do, so the drawing no longer needs its fonts.

Turn text into outlines

Use it before sending a drawing to someone without your fonts, or to reshape the letters with Edit Points.

  1. Select the text layers, or groups with text inside.
  2. Choose Type → Create Outlines (Ctrl+Shift+O).

Each text layer becomes filled paths that look exactly like the text did. One undo brings the text back.

What carries over

  • Placed as drawn. Every character goes where the browser drew it, so kerning, tracking, alignment, line spacing, paragraph wrapping, baseline shift, super/subscript and rotation all carry over. All Caps becomes capitals and Small Caps becomes smaller capitals.
  • One path per style. Each layer becomes a group named "… (outlines)", holding one path per character style in that style's fill, stroke and opacity. So a bold word or a red word is its own path. Underline and strikethrough become bars in the same paths.
  • Keeps the layer. The group takes the text's place in the stack, its transform, Layer Style effects, blend mode, opacity, lock and hidden state.

Limits

  • Characters are outlined one by one, so ligatures and the joined forms of scripts like Arabic and Devanagari aren't reproduced.
  • Small Caps uses scaled capitals rather than a font's own small caps.
  • A gradient that fills text is measured against each path rather than the whole line.
  • A bold the family doesn't have, which the browser fakes by thickening the letters, comes out at the family's nearest real weight.
  • The glyph shapes come from opentype.js, which loads the first time you create outlines.

Fonts for outlines

Create Outlines draws each letter from the real font file, so it has to get that file first.

  • Google Fonts download from Fontsource's CDN (jsDelivr). Extra character sets (Latin Extended, Cyrillic, Greek, Vietnamese) are fetched only when the text needs them.
  • Fonts installed on your computer are read directly once you've allowed installed fonts in the font picker (Chromium only).
  • System fonts otherwise use open stand-ins, and the message says which.
  • A font the browser fakes (an italic the family doesn't have) is slanted the same way.
  • If a font can't be downloaded (offline, say), that layer is left as text and the message says why.

Stand-ins

  • Arimo for Arial and Helvetica, Tinos for Times New Roman and Cousine for Courier New. These three match the originals letter for letter.
  • Gelasio for Georgia, DejaVu Sans for Verdana, Fira Sans for Trebuchet MS, Anton for Impact and Roboto for System UI.

Icons

Tools for drawing icons and app icons: a square artboard with margin guides, keylines to size shapes against, a live preview at icon sizes, and an export with every size each platform asks for. See also the pixel grid and Snap to Pixel, under Features.

File → New Icon…

Start an icon on a square artboard, with its margins already marked as guides.

  1. Choose File → New Icon….
  2. Pick a Template for the platform you're drawing for, or leave it on Custom and type a Size and Margin.
  3. Click Create (or press Enter). The icon opens in a new tab called icon-<size>, with guides shown.

Settings

  • Template: sets the size and margins from the platform's guidelines, says what the guides mean, and sets the icon preview's mask (see Templates below). Changing the size yourself goes back to Custom.
  • Size: type a size (8 to 2048 px), or pick a common one (16 to 2048) from the box's list.
  • Margin: becomes a guide on all four sides. It follows the size (a twelfth of it) until you type your own.
  • Centre guides (on by default): adds a guide across the middle each way.
  • Open the icon preview (on by default): opens Window → Icon Preview beside the canvas, masked the way the template's platform shows it.

Templates

  • Material system icon: 24 px with 2 px padding.
  • Favicon: 32 px, with a 1 px margin.
  • Android adaptive icon: 108 dp at 4× (432 px), with guides around the 72 dp area launchers show and the 66 dp safe zone inside it. Preview: circle mask, adaptive crop.
  • Google Play icon: 512 px, full bleed. Preview: rounded mask.
  • iOS app icon: 1024 px, full bleed (iOS rounds the corners itself). Preview: iOS mask.
  • macOS app icon: 1024 px with guides around the 824 px body.

Good to know

  • The margins are ordinary guides, so they move, lock, snap and save like any other guide.
  • An untouched Untitled tab gives way to the icon.

View → Icon Keylines

Size an icon's main shape so that round, square, tall and wide icons look equally big side by side.

  1. Choose View → Icon Keylines. Material's keyline shapes appear in the live area: a circle, a square, upright and wide rectangles, the diagonals and the centre lines.
  2. Size your icon's main shape to the keyline that matches it: a round icon to the circle, a tall one to the upright rectangle, and so on.
  3. Choose View → Icon Keylines again to hide them.

Good to know

  • The live area is inside the guides nearest each edge, so moving a margin guide moves the keylines. Without guides, it's a twelfth in from each edge.
  • Keylines aren't part of the drawing: they're never saved or exported.

Window → Icon Preview

See your icon at the sizes people will see it, while you draw it.

  1. Choose Window → Icon Preview (Ctrl+Alt+P). A pane docks beside the canvas (see Split view) with the drawing at 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 and 128 px.
  2. Keep drawing: the previews update as you work.
  3. Click a size to show the canvas at that size.

Options

  • Background: Light, Dark or Transparent (a checkerboard), or All three. It starts on the app's theme.
  • Mask: how platforms crop app icons. iOS is a rounded square, as iOS and macOS draw app icons. Circle and Squircle are Android launchers' shapes. Rounded rounds the corners by a fifth, as Google Play and Android do. None shows the whole square.
  • Adaptive crop: shows only the middle 72 dp of a 108 dp Android adaptive icon, the part launchers show (and mask).

Good to know

  • The button in the title bar floats the pane, and docks it back. Esc closes it.
  • Its options, whether it's docked, and how wide it is are remembered.
  • The previews are drawn by the browser just as a web page would draw the SVG.

File → Export App Icons…

Save every icon size each platform asks for, in one zip, ready to drop into a website or an app project.

  1. Draw the icon: square artwork works best (see File → New Icon…).
  2. Choose File → Export App Icons….
  3. Tick the platforms you need and pick a Background colour.
  4. Click Export. You get <name>-app-icons.zip, with a README.txt saying where each folder goes.

Each size is drawn from the vector art, not scaled from one big bitmap.

Platforms

  • Web: favicon.ico (16, 32 and 48 px), favicon.svg, apple-touch-icon.png (180), icon-192.png and icon-512.png, a site.webmanifest, and head.html, the <link> tags to paste into your pages.
  • iOS: AppIcon.appiconset (one 1024 px icon and its Contents.json) to drag into an Xcode asset catalogue.
  • Android: a res/ folder to copy into app/src/main/, and the 512 px Play Store icon. See Android adaptive icons below.
  • macOS: AppIcon.icns, and the AppIcon.iconset it's built from (16 to 1024 px), for iconutil.
  • Background: the colour for icons that can't be transparent (see Good to know) and for Android's adaptive background when there's no Background layer.

Android adaptive icons

  • The adaptive icon (Android 8+) has 108 dp foreground, background and monochrome layers for mdpi to xxxhdpi. mipmap-anydpi-v26/ic_launcher.xml and ic_launcher_round.xml tie them together.
  • The monochrome layer is the foreground's shape, for Android 13's themed icons.
  • Legacy square and round ic_launcher PNGs (48 to 192 px) are there for older launchers.
  • A layer named Background becomes the background layer, and everything else the foreground. It has to be a layer of its own, not inside a group; it's usually the bottom layer, but its place in the stack doesn't matter. Without one, the background is the Background colour (values/ic_launcher_background.xml).
  • Artwork drawn on the Android adaptive template (a 108 dp canvas, recognised by its guides 1/6 in) is used as drawn, edge to edge. The legacy and Play Store icons show its middle 72 dp, as a launcher does.
  • Any other icon's foreground is fitted into the 66 dp safe zone, so no launcher mask cuts into it, and its Background layer is stretched over the whole 108 dp so it still fills the launcher's shape.

Good to know

  • The iOS icon and the Apple touch icon can't be transparent. They're filled with the Background colour and saved without an alpha channel, as the App Store requires. So is Android's adaptive background when there's no Background layer.
  • The rest keep their transparency.
  • A non-square artboard is centred in each square icon.

Symbols

A symbol is artwork you reuse: draw it once, place it as often as you like, and change every copy at once by editing the symbol, as in Illustrator. The symbols are in the Libraries window's Symbols tab (Window → Libraries).

Make a symbol

Turn artwork you'll use again into a symbol.

  1. Select the artwork.
  2. Choose Object → Make Symbol… (or the plus button in the Symbols panel).
  3. Type a name and click Make.

The selection is replaced by one instance of the symbol, exactly where it was, so nothing moves on screen. Effects, gradients and patterns the artwork uses go with it.

Place a symbol

Add another copy (an instance) of a symbol to the drawing.

  • Click a symbol in the Libraries window's Symbols tab, then the Place (clone) button → an instance in the middle of the view.
  • Double-click a symbol → the same.
  • Drag a symbol onto the canvas → an instance where you let go.

Managing symbols

  • Rename: the pen button, or double-click the symbol's name. Instances still called after the symbol follow the new name.
  • Delete: the bin button. If the symbol has instances, you're asked whether to Break Links (the instances stay, as ordinary groups) or Delete Instances too.

Symbol instances

Use instances like any other layer, and break the link when one needs to go its own way.

  • Select, move, scale, rotate, flip, align, duplicate, lock and hide them, and set their opacity, blend mode and Layer Style.
  • The Layers panel marks them with a clover and shows the symbol's name.
  • To turn instances into ordinary groups that no longer follow the symbol, select them and choose Object → Break Link to Symbol (or the panel's broken-link button). They get their own copies of any gradients or effects inside.
  • Breaking the link of a symbol's last instance removes the symbol from the Libraries window too (Undo brings it back).

Colour

A colour you give an instance goes onto the instance, so it only shows on the parts of the symbol that don't have a colour of their own. To recolour the artwork itself, edit the symbol.

  • When every part of the symbol sets its own fill (or stroke), the Color panel shows the symbol's colour, greyed out, with an Edit Symbol link: the instance's own colour couldn't show anywhere.

Edit a symbol

Change a symbol, and every instance of it, at once.

  1. Double-click an instance (or select it and choose Object → Edit Symbol, or use the panel's nib button).
  2. The rest of the drawing dims and steps back, and the symbol's artwork appears in place of that instance. Edit it with any tool: anything you draw goes into the symbol, and every other instance follows as you work.
  3. Click Done in the bar at the top, press Esc, or double-click an empty spot to finish.

Each edit is a step in the drawing's undo history. Undoing while you edit keeps you editing.

In the file

  • Symbols are saved as real SVG <symbol> and <use> elements, so other viewers draw them too.
  • They survive saving and reopening, and copy and paste (pasting instances of a symbol the drawing already has reuses it).
  • Importing into another drawing brings them along: clashing ids are renamed and the instances follow.
  • Symbols in an imported file, including the top-level <symbol>s of icon sprite sheets, show up in the panel.
  • Define Pattern on an instance takes the symbol into the tile.

The Symbols library

Keep symbols to use in any drawing, and use the built-in icons.

  1. In the Libraries window's Symbols tab, switch from This drawing to Library.
  2. Find a symbol with the category menu and the search box, which matches names and categories.
  3. Place it with the Place (clone) button, by double-clicking it, or by dragging it onto the canvas.

Placing adds the symbol to the drawing's own symbols and puts an instance in the middle of the view, or where you drop it. From then on it's an ordinary symbol: edit it, break its link, rename it. If the drawing already has the same artwork it's reused, so placing an icon ten times gives one symbol and ten instances.

Save to the library

  • Select a symbol in This drawing (or an instance of one), then click Save to Library: the book button under This drawing, or the plus button in the Library.
  • It's copied into the library at the size it is, in the Saved category.

Managing the library

  • Rename: double-click an entry's name, or the pen button.
  • Delete: the bin button, or Alt-click the entry.
  • Reset: puts the built-in icons back. It only touches the symbols.
  • Export and Import: the library travels in the same library file as the swatches, gradients and patterns, and lives in this browser with them.

The built-in icons

  • 80 icons from Font Awesome Free 6.7.2, in eleven categories: Arrows, Shapes, Interface, Communication, Weather, People, Objects, Nature, Charts, Faces and Places.
  • They're placed 64 px tall, in the current fill colour.
  • They don't set a colour of their own, so the instance's fill paints them: select an instance and pick a colour in the Color panel to recolour it.
  • Each icon's <symbol> carries its credit (data-credit="Font Awesome Free 6.7.2 — CC BY 4.0"), so the attribution stays in any drawing that uses it.

Good to know

  • Library files are checked on the way in like any imported drawing: scripts, event handlers, javascript: links and style sheets are taken out of imported symbols.
  • Entries that don't make sense are skipped.

File Info

Give the drawing a title, an author, a description and a licence, saved in the SVG file itself in the standard way (Inkscape calls this Document Metadata).

Describe the drawing

Say what the drawing is, who made it and how others may use it.

  1. Choose File → File Info… (Alt+Shift+Ctrl+I, as in Photoshop).
  2. Fill in the fields you want.
  3. Click OK. It's one undo step and puts the * on the tab. Cancel or Esc throws the edits away.

Fields

  • Title, Author and Description: free text.
  • Keywords: comma separated.
  • Date: free text, today's date to start with. A date on its own, with every other field empty, isn't saved.
  • Copyright Status: Unknown, Copyrighted or Public Domain.
  • Copyright Notice: for example "© 2026 Your Name".
  • Licence: None, CC BY, BY-SA, BY-ND, BY-NC or BY-NC-SA 4.0, CC0 1.0, All rights reserved, or a custom URL (Licence URL).
  • Source / Info URL: where the drawing comes from, or more about it.
  • Language: a language code such as en or fr-CA.

The source and a custom licence must be http:// or https:// addresses. Anything else is refused with a note under the fields.

Good to know

  • Each tab has its own File Info, and it comes back with the tab after a reload.
  • A titled drawing's tab shows the title in its tooltip.
  • Importing or pasting an SVG into a drawing leaves the drawing's own File Info alone.
  • Copy and cut of a selection leave the File Info out, since it describes the whole drawing. Copy as SVG markup with nothing selected copies the whole file, File Info included.
  • Open reads File Info back, including from Inkscape's files (older http:// Creative Commons URLs are recognised and written back as https://). It falls back to a plain <title> / <desc>.
  • Other RDF fields Inkscape can write (publisher, contributors, identifier, relation, coverage) aren't kept: a field the dialog doesn't show is dropped when the file is saved again.

In the file

  • The title and description become the root's first <title> and <desc>. Screen readers read them, and browsers show the title as a tooltip.
  • Everything goes into a <metadata> block of RDF/XML in the shape Inkscape writes: a cc:Work with Dublin Core dc:title, dc:creator and dc:rights (each a cc:Agent), dc:date, dc:description, dc:subject (an rdf:Bag of keywords), dc:source, dc:language and cc:license.
  • A Creative Commons licence is followed by a cc:License block listing what it permits, requires and prohibits.
  • Copyright Status uses XMP's xmpRights:Marked (True copyrighted, False public domain, left out when unknown), and All rights reserved is xmpRights:UsageTerms, as Adobe's apps do.
  • The values are written with the DOM's XML APIs, so <, &, quotes and emoji are escaped properly.
  • Only text and http(s) URLs are read from a file's metadata: nothing in a <metadata> block ever enters the drawing, and none of it (or Inkscape's sodipodi:namedview) shows up as a layer.

Shortcuts

The keys follow Photoshop's. Every menu shows its commands' shortcuts, and every tooltip ends with its control's shortcut in parentheses, taken from the menus, so they always agree.

Key Action

P B E I Pen · Pencil · Eraser · Eyedropper
U · Shift+U Shape tool · next shape in the group
R O L Rectangle · Ellipse · Line
T G H Z Type · Gradient · Hand · Zoom
Space (hold) Pan
D · X Default fill and stroke (black, white) · swap them
[ ] Stroke width down / up
Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z Undo / redo (Ctrl+Y redoes too)
Ctrl+C / X / V Copy / cut / paste (as SVG)
Ctrl+J · Alt+Shift+J Layer via Copy · Layer via Cut
Ctrl+E · Ctrl+Shift+E Merge Down (Layers, Group) · Merge Visible
Ctrl+A · Ctrl+D Select all · deselect
Shift+F7 Select inverse
Alt+T · Alt+Shift+T Free Transform · Transform Again
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T Transform Again with Copy
Ctrl+G · Ctrl+Shift+G Group · ungroup
Ctrl+Alt+G (+ Shift) Make / release clipping mask
Ctrl+Shift+O Create Outlines
Ctrl+] [ · Ctrl+Shift+] [ Bring forward / send backward · to front / to back
Arrows (Shift = 10) Nudge
Del / Backspace Delete
+ − 0 1 (or Ctrl + − 0) Zoom in / out · fit · 100%
Ctrl+R · Ctrl+; · Ctrl+' Rulers · guides · grid
Ctrl+Shift+; · Ctrl+Alt+; Snap to grid · lock guides
Ctrl+Alt+I · Ctrl+Alt+C Image Size · Canvas Size
Alt+Shift+Ctrl+B Black & White…
Shift+Ctrl+U Desaturate
Tab · Shift+Tab Hide all panels · hide the right-hand panels
Ctrl+S · Ctrl+Shift+S Save · Save As…
Ctrl+O Open
Ctrl+U Show / hide the SVG source
Ctrl+Alt+P Show / hide the icon preview
Alt+Shift+Ctrl+I File Info

Shift+F10 · menu key The right-click menu of the canvas or layer

Where they differ from Photoshop

A browser keeps a few keys for itself, so these differ:

  • Free Transform is Alt+T (Ctrl+T opens a tab).
  • Layer via Cut is Alt+Shift+J (Ctrl+Shift+J opens the console in Chrome and Firefox).
  • Select Inverse is Shift+F7 (Ctrl+Shift+I opens the developer tools in some browsers).
  • New is in the File menu (Ctrl+N opens a window).
  • On a Mac, Cmd+Opt+I may open the developer tools instead of Image Size.

Good to know

  • Tab hides the panels only while you're working on the canvas (after a click on it). With a control focused it moves focus as usual, and with nothing focused it goes to the menu bar.
  • In a menu, the arrows move through it and its submenus, Home and End go to its ends, and a letter to the next command starting with it.
  • In a row of options (Type, Align, Caps…) or a panel's tabs, the arrows move along them.
  • A shortcut for a menu item that's greyed out does nothing.

SVG source

See, search and copy the drawing's SVG markup while you work, exactly as Save would write it.

Window → SVG Source

Read the SVG behind your drawing, find the markup for a layer, or copy it into a web page.

  1. Choose Window → SVG Source (Ctrl+U, as in a browser's view-source). A pane docks beside the canvas (see Split view). To change the source, click Edit (see Edit the source and New from Text).
  2. Select layers on the canvas to highlight their lines and scroll them into view. Click an element's start tag in the source to select that layer. A run inside a text layer selects the text.
  3. Click Copy to put the whole source on the clipboard, or Download to save it as an .svg file. You can also select any part of the text and copy that.
  4. Choose Window → SVG Source again, or press Esc, to close it.

Controls

  • Float (the button in the title bar): floats the pane as a window. Drag it by its title bar and resize it from its corner.
  • Find (Ctrl+F in the pane): highlights every match. Enter and Shift+Enter, or F3, step through them.
  • Wrap (on to start, remembered when you turn it off): wraps long lines instead of scrolling sideways.
  • Copy and Download: the whole source. Downloading doesn't count as saving the drawing, so the tab keeps its *.

Good to know

  • It's live: the source follows your edits, undo and tab switches. It waits while you're selecting text in it, and keeps its scroll position.
  • It includes the @import for any Google Fonts.
  • Long embedded data: URIs (images, fonts) are shortened with an … on screen, but Copy and Download give the full text. Copying a selection with the mouse copies what you see, so use Copy for those.
  • Everything in the drawing is shown as text, never run: a text layer that says <script> shows up as &lt;script&gt;, as it is in the file.
  • Large drawings stay quick: lines are drawn as they scroll into view.
  • Keys pressed inside it don't edit the drawing, apart from undo, redo, save and open (while editing, Ctrl+Z undoes your typing instead).

How it's laid out

  • It's beautified as Prettier would lay it out: one element per line, indented by nesting. A tag too long for its line gets one attribute per line.
  • Long values break where whitespace means nothing, lined up under the opening quote: path data at each M and between whole commands, points by pair, animation values and key lists at each ;, transforms by function, and style by declaration.
  • <style> CSS gets one rule per block and one declaration per line.
  • Ids, links, text and data URIs are left as they are, so Copy and Download give the same drawing, just tidier.
  • It's coloured for tags, attributes, values, comments and text. CSS (in <style> and style="") is coloured too: selectors, at-rules such as @import, properties and values.

Edit the source and New from Text

Type or paste SVG code to make a drawing, or change a drawing by editing its markup.

  • File → New from Text… → a new tab, with SVG Source open on an empty editor. Paste SVG code and click Apply (Ctrl+Enter): it becomes the drawing, as if you'd opened it as a file.
  • Edit (the pen in SVG Source) → the drawing's source as text. Change it and click Apply: the drawing is rebuilt from it, in place.
  • Cancel or Esc → back to the source view, nothing changed. Cancelling New from Text closes its empty tab.

While you type

  • The code is checked as you type. Under it, either how it reads ("Reads as SVG: 3 elements") or what's wrong, with its line and column ("Line 4, column 3: Opening and ending tag mismatch: rect and g").
  • Click the message → the line it names is selected in the text.
  • Apply waits until the code reads.
  • Tab indents; Ctrl+Z undoes your typing.

What it takes

  • A whole SVG file, <?xml …?> and comments included.
  • Shapes on their own (<circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40"/>, a few paths): they're put in an <svg> sized to fit them.
  • A web page with an <svg> in it: the first <svg> is taken out of it.

Good to know

  • Apply is one step in the History panel ("Edit Source"): Ctrl+Z puts the drawing back as it was. The selection is cleared.
  • What's applied is read as an opened file is: scripts and event handlers are taken out, animations become presets (or are reported), and SVGCraft's own layer names, locks and effects come back.
  • A New from Text drawing is named after its <title>, if it has one.
  • On a phone, SVG Source is read-only.

What the saved SVG keeps

Save writes everything you set in SVGCraft into the file itself, so opening it again, or importing it into another drawing, gives back the same editable drawing.

Saved in the file

  • Layer names, hidden layers, locks, blend modes and opacity.
  • Effects, stroke align, custom dashes and per-corner radii.
  • Clipping masks, still live and editable.
  • Gradients, patterns, styled text runs, text on a path, guides and the document size.
  • Symbols and their instances, including placed library symbols.
  • File Info: title, author, description, keywords, date, copyright and licence, as <title>, <desc> and RDF <metadata>. Open brings it back; Import leaves the receiving drawing's own (see File Info).

Not saved in the file

  • Undo history and the view: they stay with the browser's open tabs.
  • The Swatches, Gradients, Patterns and Symbols libraries: Export Library saves those.

How it's stored

  • Each setting is stored on its element, as a data-* attribute (data-sc-fx, data-sc-lock, data-name, …) or as CSS, next to real SVG (<filter>, <pattern>, <clipPath>).
  • Other viewers ignore the attributes but still draw the file correctly.
  • Editors keep attributes with their element, which comments wouldn't survive.
  • An optimiser told to strip data-* attributes keeps the look but loses the editable settings.
  • tests/roundtrip.spec.js checks all of this.
